nodes.text: And if anyone sees [us] unawares, let him keep it hidden
and deny by all the gods that he remembers:
for whoever is talkative, he will learn that she was born of blood,
he will learn that Venus [came] from the raging sea.
Yet your husband will not believe him, as a truthful
witch has promised me by her magic service.
I have seen her drawing stars down from the sky;
she turns the course of a swift river with a spell;
she with her chant splits the ground, and lures the shades from their tombs
and calls the bones down from the warm pyre;
now she holds the hellish throngs with magic shrieking,
now she orders them, sprinkled with milk, to turn back.
When she pleases, she drives the clouds from the gloomy sky;
when she pleases, she summons snow in a summer world.
She alone is said to possess Medea’s evil herbs,
she alone to have tamed the fierce hounds of Hecate.
She composed for me chants by which you could deceive:
sing them three times, and when the spells are spoken, spit three times.
He will not be able to believe anyone about us,
not even himself, if he sees [us] himself on the soft couch.
But you, keep away from others: for everything else
he will see; about me alone he will perceive nothing.
What? Should I believe it? Why, this same woman said that my love
she could dissolve with chants or herbs,
and she purified me with torches, and on a clear night
a dark victim fell to the magic gods.
I was not praying that love be wholly gone, but that it be mutual,
nor would I wish to be able to do without you.
He was made of iron who, when he could have had you,
preferred, the fool, to go after plunder and arms.
But may it be granted me to honour my fathers’ Penates
and to render the monthly incense to the ancient Lar.
How well they lived when Saturn was king, before
the earth was opened up into long roads!
Not yet had the pine scorned the blue waves
and offered a spread sail to the winds,
nor had the roving sailor, seeking profit in unknown lands,
loaded his ship with foreign goods.
In that age the strong bull did not go under the yoke,
the horse did not champ the bit with tamed mouth,
no house had doors, no stone was fixed in the fields
to rule the plough-lands with sure boundaries.
Yet be merciful, by the pacts of our secret bed,
by Venus, I beg, and by your head laid beside mine.
I am the one who, when you lay worn out by grim sickness,
am said to have snatched you away by my vows,
and I myself purified you all round with pure sulphur,
after an old woman had first chanted a magic spell;
I myself took care that cruel dreams could not
harm you, dreams to be averted three times with holy meal;
I myself, veiled with a fillet and with loosened tunic,
made nine vows to Trivia in the silent night.
I paid them all: now another enjoys your love,
and, lucky man, he reaps the profit of my prayers.
Often I held another, but just as I was approaching the joys,
Venus reminded me of my mistress and deserted me.
Then the woman, leaving, said I was bewitched,
and — it shames me — tells that my girl knows unspeakable things.
She does not do this with words: with her face and tender arms
and her golden hair my girl bewitches [me].
Such was the Nereid who once, to Haemonian Peleus,
was carried, blue Thetis, on a bridled fish.
These things have harmed me: that a rich lover is at hand for her;
a cunning bawd has come for my ruin.
May she eat bloody meals and with gory mouth
drink bitter cups mixed with much gall;
may souls flit round her bewailing their fates,
and may the fierce screech owl sing always from the roofs;
may she herself, raging under the goad of hunger, seek herbs on graves
and bones left behind by savage wolves,
may she run with bare groin and howl through the cities,
and a rough pack of dogs from the crossroads drive her on behind.
It will come to pass: the god gives signs; lovers have their divinities,
and Venus, deserted on unjust terms, rages.
But you, as soon as you can, the teachings of the grasping witch
abandon, for every love is won by gifts.
The poor man will always be at your side; the poor man will approach you
first and will cling to your tender side,
She pleases, though she has come with unadorned face
and has not dressed her shining hair with lingering art.
Has some old woman, with spells, with pale herbs,
bewitched you in the silent time of night?
Song draws crops away from neighbouring fields,
song halts the path of the angry snake,
song tries to draw the Moon down from her chariot,
and would do it, if struck bronzes did not ring out.
Why, alas, do I complain that a spell has harmed the poor wretch, why [blame] herbs?
Beauty has no use for magic aids:
what does the harm is to have touched her body, to have given long
kisses, to have pressed thigh against thigh.
